description:
Aksum Orbit is a team of developers from Addis Ababa, who are beginning to work on a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, an interactive game for children to learn about how astronauts go through training. Our idea comes from the great engineering skills of the Aksum period from Ethiopia and the idea of space exploration in the future.

We are looking for people who love game development, web development, graphic design, animation, writing and storytelling.
summary:
Aksum Orbit is a  lunar mission simulator and junior astronaut training platform for children aged 7–12. We developed an interactive 10-day Moon South Pole expedition where players command a six-member astronaut crew, manage oxygen, water, food, and solar energy, and make critical survival decisions.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming authentic space science into engaging, child-friendly gameplay. It integrates NASA DONKI space-weather data, RadLab radiation research, and lunar terrain data to create realistic mission challenges. Inspired by ancient Aksumite engineering, players build solar-tracking Great Stele structures, Mai Shum-inspired water recycling systems, and underground regolith radiation shields.

Aksum Orbit is important because it makes space education more accessible through multilingual learning, adaptive difficulty, motion-based simulations, audio captions, voice navigation, and an AI learning copilot. By connecting African heritage with modern lunar exploration, Aksum Orbit empowers children to overcome language and educational barriers while developing scientific thinking, problem-solving skills, and the confidence to become tomorrow's space explorers.
details:
Project Details: Aksum Orbit

Aksum Orbit is an interactive lunar mission simulator that transforms children into junior astronauts commanding a 10-day expedition at the Moon's South Pole. Players lead a six-member crew, manage four essential life-support resources (oxygen, water, food, and solar power), construct lunar infrastructure, and respond to mission emergencies. Each decision affects crew survival, teaching children how real space missions depend on science, planning, and teamwork.

The project combines NASA open data, including DONKI space-weather information, RadLab radiation research, and lunar terrain data, to create science-inspired challenges. Players construct solar-tracking Great Stele structures, Mai Shum-inspired water recycling systems, and underground regolith shields to protect their lunar base from environmental hazards.

Our platform promotes inclusive STEM education through English, Amharic, and Afaan Oromoo support, two difficulty levels, physical motion simulations, audio captions, speech-to-text navigation, and the Aksum Orbit AI copilot, which explains scientific concepts and guides players through challenges.

Our intended impact: is to make space science accessible to children regardless of their language, reading ability, or educational background. We aim to develop scientific curiosity, critical thinking, resource management, and problem-solving skills while inspiring the next generation of African space explorers.

Technology and tools: The project is designed as a browser-based application using web development technologies, NASA open-data resources, AI-assisted learning, and interactive simulation systems. The specific programming languages, frameworks, and development tools are those used in our implementation.

Creativity and innovation: Our central innovation is connecting ancient Aksumite engineering wisdom with futuristic lunar survival technology. Rather than presenting space science as a textbook lesson, we turn it into a playable survival experience where African heritage becomes part of the solution to real scientific challenges.

During development, we considered scientific relevance, age appropriateness, accessibility, multilingual inclusion, gameplay engagement, data integration, and technical feasibility. Our goal is simple: make every child feel that becoming a space explorer is possible.
